## Jougla Point on an Antarctic expedition: a possible landing near Port Lockroy

[Jougla Point](/antarctica/place/jougla-point/) lies along the western edge of Wiencke Island in the [Port Lockroy](/antarctica/place/port-lockroy/) area. Low rocky stretches are surrounded by snow, glaciers and cold seawater. Gentoo penguins and blue-eyed shags nest along the shore, and seals can be seen in the area. Traces of Antarctica's human history also make the location interesting: whale bones remain on the shore as reminders of the whaling industry.

We consider a visit to this site on two [11-day Antarctic expeditions](/antarctica/tour/). This is **a possible stop on the itinerary**, not a separate guaranteed excursion that can be added to a cruise on a fixed timetable. The program takes account of Antarctic weather, sea ice, coastal conditions and protected-area restrictions.

## Which trips may include a visit?

[Antarctica: Discovery and Learning](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/) sails from [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/) across the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/) to the Antarctic Peninsula and the [South Shetland Islands](/antarctica/place/south-shetland-islands/). Sea and shore activities are concentrated in the Antarctic portion on days 4–7. Possible sites include [Danco Island](/antarctica/place/danco-island/), Neko Harbour, Paradise Bay, the Port Lockroy area and Jougla Point. **None of these individual landings is unconditionally assigned to a particular day.**

The second program, [Antarctica: Discovery and Long Hikes](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-long-hikes-11-days/), also offers the possibility of visiting the Jougla area. It places additional emphasis on walking routes in suitable conditions, including potential snowshoeing near nearby Damoy Point. This is **a different potential activity**, not automatically a hike on Jougla Point. The exact site and appropriate level of exertion are determined on board.

Both tours last 11 days and 10 nights. When choosing between them, compare the advertised activities and departure dates rather than focusing on a single geographic name.

## What travelers may see at Jougla Point

Gentoo penguins gather on sections of rocky shore, while blue-eyed shags nest in areas accessible to the birds. Weddell seals can also appear nearby. These are wildlife-watching opportunities, **not promises to encounter every species**. Birds move between the water and land, and some areas close to protect nesting colonies.

Narrow bays, rocks and icy slopes highlight the contrast between a small coastal headland and the broad panorama seen from an expedition ship. When conditions allow, guides arrange a safe route ashore, but the accessible areas may change even within a single season.

Nearby [Goudier Island](/antarctica/place/goudier-island/) is home to historic Port Lockroy. The former British base is known for its museum and post office. The opportunity to visit the museum and the possibility of landing at Jougla Point are **two separate decisions**: stopping at one site does not guarantee a landing at the other.

## Why a landing may be replaced

The expedition team assesses wind, swells, ice and conditions at the landing site. The shore may be inaccessible to Zodiacs, while certain areas must sometimes be avoided to protect birds. Even when the ship is in the Port Lockroy area, passengers cannot automatically go ashore.

International rules for Antarctic visits require keeping a safe distance from wildlife, neither touching nor feeding birds, following guides' instructions and staying within marked boundaries. Protecting nature matters more than ticking off a famous headland at any cost. If conditions change, the team may choose another accessible site, a boat excursion or observation from the ship.

Travelers should distinguish **the geography of a possible itinerary** from **a guaranteed service**. Lists of islands and bays describe the character of the expedition; the final order of visits is determined on location.

## Choosing an expedition with Jougla Point in mind

If birds, coastal landings and the expedition team's work interest you most, consider the [Discovery and Learning program](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/). If you want more physical activity and the possibility of longer walks, compare the [hiking-focused expedition](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-long-hikes-11-days/). Do not choose the second option solely because you expect a hike near Jougla: snowshoe routes and coastal visits depend on conditions.

When booking, discuss the season, cabin categories, length of sea crossings and participant requirements for walking activities. Bring layered wind-resistant clothing and follow instructions on cleaning footwear and equipment before going ashore. The full equipment list and permitted activities are specified for each voyage.

## Frequently asked questions about Jougla Point

### Is Jougla Point guaranteed on the expedition?

On our two 11-day programs, it remains a possible route stop. A landing depends on weather, ice, shore accessibility and expedition-team decisions.

### Can you book a separate excursion to the point during the cruise?

No fixed standalone excursion to Jougla is advertised on these programs. A visit is considered within the wider flexible expedition itinerary.

### Are gentoo penguins guaranteed?

They nest in the Jougla Point area, but actual observations depend on the season, accessible sites and bird behavior. If animals are encountered, visitors keep the distances set by guides.

### Does a visit to Jougla include the Port Lockroy museum?

These are nearby but separate sites. The opportunity to visit the museum on Goudier Island and a landing at Jougla Point are considered independently.

## King George Island: research stations, flights and routes through Antarctica

[King George Island](/antarctica/place/king-george-island/) is the largest island in the [South Shetland Islands](/antarctica/place/south-shetland-islands/) archipelago, north of the Antarctic Peninsula. Its western section, the Fildes Peninsula, is associated with an Antarctic airfield and several international research stations. Visitors see a combination rarely found in the region: scientific infrastructure, rocky shores, glaciers and seabirds.

Two travel formats should be distinguished. **A fly-in trip** allows visitors to arrive from southern Chile and spend time on King George Island. **An air-cruise** uses the island as a transfer point to an expedition ship, which then sails to other islands and shores of the [Antarctic Peninsula](/antarctica/place/antarctic-peninsula/). The amount of time spent on King George Island differs substantially between these formats.

## How to reach King George Island

Teniente Marsh Airfield, near Chile's [Frei Station](/antarctica/place/frei-station/), is used for flights into the Antarctic region. Punta Arenas in [Chile](/chile/place/punta-arenas/) is the departure point on certain Ada Tours programs. An accompanying team meets visitors after landing, and the next steps depend on the chosen itinerary.

For example, the [8-day Classic Antarctica program](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/) includes a flight to King George Island, a walk through the station area and boarding a Zodiac for transfer to the expedition ship. Days exploring the South Shetland Islands and the western shores of the peninsula follow. In this program, King George Island serves primarily as the gateway to a sea expedition.

The [overnight program](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/) has a different structure: after flying to the island, visitors explore local sites, including nearby [Ardley Island](/antarctica/place/ardley-island/) and [Collins Glacier](/antarctica/place/collins-glacier/), then spend the night in an equipped ice camp. This suits travelers who want to spend more time on King George Island itself.

| Format | Main feature |
|---|---|
| Fly-in trip | Visiting the island and surrounding area |
| Air-cruise | Transferring to a ship and continuing the route |
| Overnight program | Additional time on the island itself |

## What you can see on the island

King George Island is known for international scientific research. Research stations stand in different parts of the island, and the Fildes area contains sites also mentioned in tourist itineraries. Visiting a station does not mean unrestricted access to its working buildings: research facilities have their own safety requirements and schedules.

Confirmed Ada Tours itineraries mention [Frei Station](/antarctica/place/frei-station/), the Russian [Bellingshausen Station](/antarctica/place/bellingshausen-station/), [Great Wall Station](/antarctica/place/great-wall-station/) and [Villa Las Estrellas](/antarctica/place/villa-las-estrellas/). The Orthodox church at Bellingshausen is also noted. Whether each site can be visited depends on the itinerary, weather and necessary permissions.

Beyond the stations, [Collins Glacier](/antarctica/place/collins-glacier/) and coastal bays are highlights. Zodiac boats take visitors toward nearby [Ardley Island](/antarctica/place/ardley-island/) to watch penguins. Parts of Ardley are strictly protected, so landings are not allowed everywhere. Seals, penguins and seabirds also inhabit the shores and waters of the South Shetland Islands, with sightings varying by season.

## Scientific Antarctica and visitor rules

King George Island offers a glimpse of how people work in polar weather: researchers study the atmosphere, ocean, ice and wildlife here. These are active scientific facilities, however, not museum districts. Photographing a station from a permitted location and entering a laboratory are quite different privileges.

Conservation rules also cover beaches, breeding colonies and vegetated areas. When watching birds, do not obstruct routes between nests and the sea, approach animals for a photograph or ignore guides' instructions. Before landing, footwear and equipment are cleaned to reduce the risk of transferring non-native organisms between coastal sites.

## Choosing an itinerary: island or peninsula

Prioritizing King George Island makes sense if you are interested in research stations, flying to Antarctica, coastal walks, penguins and possibly staying overnight on the island. For a longer introduction to icy fjords and sea channels, compare [Antarctic cruises](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/tours/antarctica/) and routes toward the [Gerlache Strait](/antarctica/place/gerlache-strait/) or [Penola Strait](/antarctica/place/penola-strait/).

On the [8-day air-cruise](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/), different peninsula locations are listed as possibilities rather than guaranteed stops on every departure. On the shorter overnight trip, visits are concentrated around King George Island. Comparing programs simply by the word "Antarctica" or by price would therefore be misleading: their transportation arrangements and actual days in the south differ fundamentally.

## When to travel and what may change the plan

Expedition travel is generally planned for the Southern Hemisphere summer. Even then, wind, cloud cover and sea conditions can alter flight schedules, Zodiac embarkation and access to particular shores. Extra time before and after the Antarctic portion is particularly useful when flying.

Before purchasing, check duration, permitted aircraft luggage, mandatory briefings, flight-rescheduling terms, accommodation and included services. These details differ between products. Ada Tours can help compare itineraries and arrange the sequence of your journey, taking account of time in the south and weather risks.

## Frequently asked questions about King George Island

### Can you fly to King George Island without crossing the Drake Passage by sea?

Yes. Some programs offer flights from Punta Arenas. Other expeditions arrive by sea; the method depends on the selected tour.

### Do tourists always visit the research stations?

No. Visits depend on the itinerary, permits and the station's operations. A station's appearance in an island description guarantees nothing by itself.

### Is it better to spend the night on the island or aboard ship?

These are different formats. Only the relevant programs include an overnight stay on the island; cruises provide shipboard accommodation. Compare the terms of each specific tour.

### Are King George Island and the Antarctic Peninsula the same place?

No. King George Island belongs to the South Shetland Islands north of the Antarctic Peninsula. An air-cruise may link them in one journey.

## Which tours through King George Island should you choose?

[King George Island](/antarctica/place/king-george-island/) lies in the South Shetland Islands archipelago, northwest of the Antarctic Peninsula. It serves two purposes for visitors. They fly here from Punta Arenas in Chile to start or finish an expedition cruise, and they also come for research stations, glaciers and penguins.

**The inclusion of King George Island on an itinerary does not indicate how much time you will spend on the island itself.** On one tour it is the main setting for land excursions; on another it is a transfer point between aircraft and ship. The best way to choose is therefore by arrival method, length of stay and what the Antarctic itinerary includes.

Our selection contains {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} featuring King George Island among the main route destinations.

| Tour | What sets it apart |
|---|---|
| [Antarctica Day Trip](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-day-tour-from-punta-arenas/) | Fly to the island and return to Chile on the same day |
| [Antarctica Overnight Adventure](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-adventure/) | 2 days in Antarctica, one night in camp |
| [Overnight Program](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/) | 5-day full package with an overnight stay on the island |
| [Classic Antarctica](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/) | 8 days, flight and expedition cruise |
| [Antarctica Express](/multi-country/tour/antarctica-patagonia-express-air-cruise-6-days/) | 6 days, sea journey from Ushuaia and return flight from the island |

The table highlights the main differences between formats. Nights in Punta Arenas and the time spent in Antarctica itself may be counted separately. Always compare total duration, flights and accommodation in each tour's detailed description.

## King George Island: a separate island or the Antarctic Peninsula?

It is **an island in the South Shetland Islands archipelago**, near the Antarctic Peninsula, not a part of continental Antarctica. This geography explains why arrival points, polar stations and short fly-in trips are concentrated here.

The island contains ice-covered areas, exposed rocky shores and scientific infrastructure. Stations belonging to different countries are nearby, including [Bellingshausen](/antarctica/place/bellingshausen-station/), [Frei](/antarctica/place/frei-station/) and [Great Wall](/antarctica/place/great-wall-station/). They make King George Island especially interesting to people who want to see how humans live and work in the polar region.

Nature excursions reveal another side of the island. Ada Tours programs mention [Ardley Island](/antarctica/place/ardley-island/) with its penguin colonies and [Collins Glacier](/antarctica/place/collins-glacier/). Boat trips and access to particular shores depend on weather and visitor regulations.

If the goal is to **set foot on the continental mainland of Antarctica**, rather than an island in the South Shetlands, check the specific landings scheduled or possible on the expedition cruise. Simply arriving on King George Island does not mean you will land on the mainland.

## Flying from Punta Arenas: one day or an overnight stay

The shortest of these trips to the island is the [day trip from Punta Arenas](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-day-tour-from-punta-arenas/). The plane brings the group to King George Island, where the land program is planned to include the Villa Las Estrellas area, a church beside Bellingshausen Station, a Zodiac outing toward Ardley and navigation near Collins Glacier. The Antarctic portion lasts approximately five hours, after which a flight back to Chile is scheduled if weather permits.

This is **one day in Antarctica**, but the arrangements also include prior arrival in Punta Arenas, a briefing and accommodation. "One day on the island" should not be treated as the full door-to-door duration of the journey.

For travelers who want to stay overnight, there is the [Unforgettable Antarctica Tour](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-adventure/). According to its description, the Antarctic segment lasts 2 days and 1 night. On day one, the plan includes the flight, exploring the island, boat outings and Collins Glacier. The night is spent at an equipped camp. The next day continues around the elephant seal colony and the Chinese [Great Wall Station](/antarctica/place/great-wall-station/), before the group flies to Punta Arenas. The program describes small flight groups of 5 to 6 passengers aboard a Beechcraft King Air 300.

[Another overnight program](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/) covers similar island geography but lists **5 days and 4 nights for the entire itinerary**, including accommodation in Punta Arenas. When comparing them, check how many of those days are spent in Antarctica and how many are allocated to preparation and waiting for the flight in Chile.

## King George Island as the beginning of an air-cruise

On the [8-day Classic Antarctica air-cruise](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/), the island has a different function. Travelers fly from Punta Arenas to King George Island and, after landing, walk toward the shore through the Frei and Bellingshausen station areas. A Zodiac then takes them to the expedition ship.

The main experiences on this itinerary take place at sea. Depending on conditions, the ship explores the waters around the Antarctic Peninsula and South Shetland Islands. Passengers observe icebergs, seabirds and marine wildlife, join boat excursions and make landings where possible. The potential route includes the [Gerlache Strait](/antarctica/place/gerlache-strait/) and other waterways, but passage through any specific strait is not guaranteed in advance.

After the sea expedition, the group returns to King George Island for the flight back to Punta Arenas. This option suits travelers who see the island as **the entry point to a larger sea expedition**, rather than somewhere to spend two nights on land.

Compare it with the [cruises and expeditions catalog](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/): some itineraries use the island as an air hub, while others travel entirely by sea.

## By sea across the Drake Passage, returning by air

The [6-day Antarctica Express](/multi-country/tour/antarctica-patagonia-express-air-cruise-6-days/) takes a different direction. The expedition starts in Ushuaia, Argentina, travels through the Beagle Channel and the Cape Horn area, then crosses the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/) to the South Shetland Islands.

King George Island appears toward the end of the journey. The ship arrives in the Fildes Bay area; after disembarking, the group makes its way to the aircraft through the Frei and Bellingshausen station area. The return to Punta Arenas is by air, avoiding a second sea crossing of the Drake Passage.

This option suits travelers who **want to experience the sea crossing from Ushuaia** but do not plan to repeat it on the return journey. Its logistics differ from a return-flight option: the trip starts and ends in different cities and countries, and sea conditions may affect the expedition timetable.

Importantly, King George Island serves primarily as **the place where the Antarctic sailing ends and the return flight departs**, so it is not equivalent to programs with overnight stays and island excursions.

## What can you see on the island?

If the chosen tour allocates time for land excursions, natural and scientific sites are the main attractions. [Bellingshausen](/antarctica/place/bellingshausen-station/) and [Frei](/antarctica/place/frei-station/) are associated with the life and transportation of polar expeditions. The [Great Wall Station](/antarctica/place/great-wall-station/) area introduces visitors to China's presence in Antarctica. Entry to active research stations is subject to permits; an itinerary that names a station does not guarantee access to its buildings.

For wildlife watching, programs use Zodiac boats near [Ardley Island](/antarctica/place/ardley-island/). Keeping a safe distance from penguins, observing landing restrictions and following guides' recommendations are essential. At [Collins Glacier](/antarctica/place/collins-glacier/), visitors are drawn to ice formations and views of the coast.

These sites may appear on the same short itinerary, but **weather determines which outings actually take place**. Wind and sea state are important for boat trips, while visibility and other flying conditions matter for aircraft. When choosing a tour, find out which activities are planned on the island and which remain weather-dependent alternatives.

## How to choose the right format

Begin with one question: **why do you want to visit King George Island in particular?**

If you would like to spend a day among research stations and penguins, explore the [day trip](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-day-tour-from-punta-arenas/). If an Antarctic night is important to you, compare the [2-day Antarctic portion](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-adventure/) and the [5-day full package](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/), taking care to distinguish nights on the island from those in Punta Arenas.

If marine wildlife, icebergs and several days aboard an expedition ship are your priorities, the [8-day air-cruise](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/) makes more sense. To combine Ushuaia, Cape Horn, the Drake Passage and a one-way return flight, consider [Antarctica Express](/multi-country/tour/antarctica-patagonia-express-air-cruise-6-days/).

The wider choice is in the [Antarctic tour catalog](/antarctica/tour/). First compare the route, number of days in Antarctica, included flights and potential changes due to weather.

## Frequently asked questions about tours through King George Island

### Can you visit Antarctica without crossing the Drake Passage by sea?

Yes. The [day trip](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-day-tour-from-punta-arenas/), [overnight programs](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/) and [8-day air-cruise](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/) include a flight from Punta Arenas to King George Island. The air-cruise then continues as a sea expedition around the Antarctic Peninsula.

### Does visiting the island mean I will set foot on continental Antarctica?

No. King George Island is part of the South Shetland Islands. To land specifically on the continental shore, check the expedition ship's landing sites and weather-dependent alternatives.

### Which tour lets you spend the night on the island itself?

King George Island overnight stays are included in the [Unforgettable Antarctica Tour](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-adventure/) and the [overnight program](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/). Their descriptions list total package duration and any additional nights in Punta Arenas separately.

### Where is the airport relative to the research stations?

It is on King George Island near Frei Station. The [Classic Antarctica](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/) itinerary describes an approximately 2 km walk through the Frei and Bellingshausen area to the Zodiac boarding point. The actual sequence depends on organizational arrangements for the voyage.

### Are Zodiac trips to see penguins guaranteed?

No. Zodiac outings toward [Ardley Island](/antarctica/place/ardley-island/) are included in several short programs, but whether they take place depends on wind, sea conditions and conservation regulations.

### How does the weather affect fly-in tours?

Weather can change flight departure and landing times as well as land excursions. Planning should therefore account for the mandatory advance briefing and the itinerary's terms regarding accommodation and possible schedule changes.

## Lemaire Channel: an Antarctic cruise between icy cliffs

The Lemaire Channel lies off the western coast of the [Antarctic Peninsula](/antarctica/place/antarctic-peninsula/). The mountains of Booth Island rise on one side, and the slopes of Graham Land on the other. The main experience here is the navigation itself: towering walls, a narrow ribbon of water and blocks of ice that can sometimes close off the passage.

Lemaire is included in expedition itineraries primarily for the views from the ship. Unlike an island stop, sailing through the channel does not itself involve a landing. The captain decides whether to enter, the speed of travel and the onward course according to ice and wind conditions.

## Where Lemaire is and why it is famous

The channel separates Booth Island from the coast of Graham Land. It is approximately 11 km long. The shores come so close together that the waterway feels like a narrow mountain gorge. Snowy slopes, reflections on calm water and the size of the icebergs make each voyage different from the last.

The landscape depends on light, clouds and the amount of drifting ice. Sometimes a ship can pass through open water. On another day, ice may block the corridor so completely that turning around is safer. Photographs taken in one season do not guarantee that the passage will be navigable on the dates of another cruise.

## Which islands lie farther south?

On some routes, Lemaire links the peninsula's northern areas with islands farther south. Nearby sites include [Pléneau Island](/antarctica/place/pleneau-island/) and [Petermann Island](/antarctica/place/petermann-island/). Passing through the channel does not imply a landing on both islands: each shore has its own approach conditions.

On Ada Tours' [Antarctica: Beyond the Antarctic Circle](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-polar-circle-deep-south-13-days/) itinerary, navigation through Lemaire toward Pléneau and Petermann is one possible option for the Antarctic portion. In favorable ice conditions, the expedition may continue along the [Argentine Islands](/antarctica/place/argentine-islands/) toward [Crystal Sound](/antarctica/place/crystal-sound/). The distribution of sites across days depends on actual conditions.

When comparing routes, distinguish three descriptions:

- **Passing through Lemaire:** The ship actually sails the length of the channel when navigation is safe.
- **Approaching Lemaire:** Passengers see the entrance, but the vessel may change course.
- **Landing on a neighboring island:** A separate activity restricted by ice, weather and conservation requirements.

If you are traveling for a particular photograph or island, check which of these activities the itinerary actually describes.

## What can be seen from the ship?

Lemaire is notable for its mountain geography and sea ice. From relatively close up, passengers can see rock walls and glaciers, while icebergs of various shapes float in the water. Seabirds and Antarctic wildlife may appear along the way, but a whale or seal encounter cannot be promised at a certain stretch or time.

For photography, a spare battery, protection against moisture and a lens that captures a wide landscape can be helpful. Wind is stronger on the open deck. During difficult navigation, passenger access to certain areas of the ship may be restricted.

## Who discovered the channel?

Carl Dallmann's German expedition spotted this coastal stretch in 1873–1874. Adrien de Gerlache's Belgian expedition passed through the channel and charted it in 1898. Its name honors Charles Lemaire, who helped organize Belgian exploration. The initial discovery and documented passage therefore belong to different expeditions.

## Assessing the likelihood of passage when booking

First establish the role Lemaire plays in the selected itinerary: a principal geographic objective, one possible route for expedition navigation, or a named landmark. Then consider how much time is allocated to the Antarctic portion and which areas could replace the channel if ice makes it inaccessible.

The expedition team makes decisions about navigation and shore visits based on weather, safety, ice and environmental rules. We can help you compare the named locations and trip durations. Other travel formats are described in [Cruises and Expeditions](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/).

## Frequently asked questions about the Lemaire Channel

### Is passage through the channel guaranteed?

No. Drifting ice and weather can make the narrow waterway inaccessible. The captain makes the decision.

### Do you need to land to see Lemaire?

No. The main attraction is navigation and the view from the deck. Landings on nearby islands are considered separately.

### What lies south of the channel?

Depending on the route, the next sites may include [Pléneau](/antarctica/place/pleneau-island/), [Petermann](/antarctica/place/petermann-island/) and the waters near the [Argentine Islands](/antarctica/place/argentine-islands/).

### Are the Lemaire Channel and Lemaire Island the same place?

No. The channel lies between Booth Island and Graham Land. The island with the same name is on a different stretch of the peninsula's coastline.

## Lemaire Channel: a possible passage on the way to the Antarctic Circle

The [Lemaire Channel](/antarctica/place/lemaire-channel/) runs between Booth Island and the western coast of Graham Land near the Antarctic Peninsula. It is a narrow waterway between tall, snow-covered slopes. Water, rock walls and floating ice create a landscape best appreciated directly from a ship's deck.

On the [13-day Antarctica: Beyond the Antarctic Circle expedition](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-polar-circle-deep-south-13-days/), Lemaire remains **a possible section of navigation**. The ship will pass through if ice and navigational conditions permit. It is not a guaranteed standalone excursion or shore landing. The captain and expedition team decide whether passage is safe.

## The channel's role on the route

The cruise starts in [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/), sails through the Beagle Channel and [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/) and then explores the shores of the [Antarctic Peninsula](/antarctica/place/antarctic-peninsula/). During days 4–10, the ship moves between accessible natural sites, bays and islands. If ice permits, the route may pass through Lemaire toward [Pléneau Island](/antarctica/place/pleneau-island/) and [Petermann Island](/antarctica/place/petermann-island/).

Near Pléneau and Petermann, passengers may watch birds and wildlife characteristic of the Antarctic islands. Sailing through Lemaire does not, however, guarantee landing on either island. Every Zodiac outing or shore visit during an expedition depends on access and the conditions of the day.

The longer-term aim is the Antarctic Circle. **Crossing the circle also depends on suitable ice conditions.** It would therefore be wrong to promise passengers that they will definitely experience the Lemaire Channel, particular islands and an Antarctic Circle crossing.

## What you see from the ship

Lemaire's main feature is the confined passage between snowy rocky shores. Depending on the light, passengers may see shades of ice on the slopes, mountain reflections in the water and individual floes. The ship passes through only when it can maneuver safely: the channel's narrowness demands close attention to ice conditions.

Unlike landings on islands, Lemaire is interesting for **the ship's movement through the scenery itself**. There is no need to find a trail or wait for a transfer ashore. Sometimes the best views are from the outer deck, but the crew sets passenger access to open areas, photography rules and safe viewing points.

According to an Antarctic geographical gazetteer, the channel separates Booth Island from the Graham Land coast. Adrien de Gerlache's Belgian Antarctic Expedition passed through it in 1898. Its name honors explorer Charles Lemaire. Modern voyages take place in much greater comfort, but the dependence on sea ice remains.

## What happens if there is too much ice?

Even in the Antarctic summer, drifting ice may partially block the channel. Any attempt to enter takes account of the ship, visibility, wind and the distribution of ice floes. In difficult conditions, the expedition changes the order of visits and chooses alternative bays or islands.

This does not mean the whole Antarctic portion disappears: the main stages cover a wider area of the peninsula, with opportunities to observe seabirds, glaciers and wildlife. However, the exact sites reached are determined on the spot. The actual route may differ from the preliminary list of possible stops.

When choosing a trip, it makes more sense to assess duration, the general cruising area and the available activities than to let the decision depend on one narrow channel.

## Comparing Lemaire with other experiences

If **seascapes and traveling toward southern latitudes** are your priority, the [13-day Antarctic Circle itinerary](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-polar-circle-deep-south-13-days/) provides that format. If you dream of penguin colonies and observing wildlife ashore, compare possible stops at [Livingston Island](/antarctica/place/livingston-island/) and other islands; these landings are separate activities and depend on prevailing conditions.

For an overall comparison of durations and formats, visit the [Antarctic tours catalog](/antarctica/tour/) and [Cruises and Expeditions](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/). Sailing past icy cliffs, taking a short Zodiac outing and landing ashore are distinct travel experiences. When choosing, clarify which are possibilities and which are fixed parts of the itinerary.

## Frequently asked questions about the Lemaire Channel

### Is passage through Lemaire guaranteed on the 13-day expedition?

No. It is listed only when ice conditions allow; the captain may choose another route.

### Is there a landing within the channel itself?

Lemaire is described as a navigational section of the voyage. Shore visits take place at other potential itinerary sites and require separate safe conditions.

### Will there be landings on Pléneau or Petermann islands after Lemaire?

These islands are possible onward destinations. The expedition team decides whether they can actually be visited and whether landings are possible.

### If the ship cannot pass through Lemaire, is it certain to cross the Antarctic Circle?

No. Crossing the Antarctic Circle also depends on ice and navigational opportunities. Both conditions should be considered when choosing dates and a voyage.
